title: Stockton, 1912
hookLine: Sikh farmworkers open the first gurdwara in the United States in California
carry: a door in a new land

lines: FARMERS WHO KNOW WATER AND SOIL.
cards: California's Central Valley, about 1910. Flat fields to the horizon, heat shimmering off the dirt.
Men from Punjab, many of them Sikh, have come down from Canada and across from Asia to pick fruit, clear land and dig irrigation ditches.

It's familiar work: Punjab means five rivers, and these are farmers who know water and soil. But on a Sunday, there's nowhere to go. The nearest gurdwara is far up the coast in Vancouver, days away by train.
So a few of them decide to make one.

teach.b: In 1912, Sikh farmworkers formed the Pacific Coast Khalsa Diwan Society and opened a gurdwara in Stockton, a Central Valley farm town. It was the first gurdwara in the United States.

It began modestly; years later a new building went up beside the first. For decades it was the only one in the country, where Sikhs came from all over the West for gurpurabs, weddings and news from home.
Gurdwara: gur, the Guru; dwara, a door. The Guru's door.

teach.h: A SANGAT, A MEAL, A MEETING PLACE.
teach.b: Through Stockton's door, lonely men found a sangat, a hot meal at langar, a bed for the night. Politics came through it too.
Some Sikhs and other Indians in California were campaigning for India's freedom from British rule, and the gurdwara became a meeting place for them.

Life outside the door was hard. Laws kept most Indian women from coming, and restricted who the men could marry and whether they could own land. In southern California, many Punjabi men married Mexican women.
Their children grew up in families that mixed Punjabi and Spanish, gurdwara and church; they were sometimes called Mexican-Hindus, and some came to Stockton for the big gatherings.

teach.h: A DOOR IN A NEW LAND.
teach.b: This week ran from the library that was lost, through November 1984, the long wait, how the panth remembers, leaving Punjab and the sawmills, to Stockton: from loss to a door opened in a new land.

how: Gurdwaras across the United States welcome visitors to kirtan and langar; the Stockton gurdwara, the oldest in the country, still serves a sangat today.

practice: If you have your phone, look up the nearest gurdwara and find it on a map, how far it is and what street it's on; you don't have to go.
Then put the phone down and picture its door, open, with shoes lined up outside and someone serving tea inside. Think of the farmworkers in Stockton who made the first one.
